subject: Network handoff decision for Acacia pilot: Direct peering vs private interface vs encrypted tunnel
messages:
From: Rajiv Narayan <rajiv@acaciahealth.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: networking@acaciahealth.com
Date: 2026-06-27T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Pilot connectivity options — quick scoping questions

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. We're starting to scope the private deployment pilot for one of our analytics workloads and want alignment on the network handoff. High level: 2x GPU instances in our VPC, expected 100–150 TPS (small requests), strict P95 latency target ~60ms from our app tier, and strict controls on cross-account egress.

Key questions we need answered before procurement:
- Which connectivity mode gives us the best isolation + predictable latency (VPC peering, interface endpoint/PrivateLink, or S2S VPN)?
- What are the operational tradeoffs for cross-account IAM and IP ownership? We need to avoid exposing server IPs to multiple owners.
- Any gotchas around TCP session affinity, MTU fragmentation, and long-lived KV cache updates?

Can your team produce a short recommendation and a checklist we can use with our netops? We have a tight window to commit reserved capacity if the connectivity choice looks good.

Appreciate it — happy to hop on a call with your architects.

— Rajiv
Head of Platform Engineering
Acacia Health

From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
To: Rajiv Narayan <rajiv@acaciahealth.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, marcus_lin@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-06-27T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pilot connectivity options — quick scoping questions

Rajiv — thanks, this is a great summary. We put an initial playbook together (attached) and sketched three operational patterns. Short answer up front: for your constraints I recommend a hybrid approach (interface endpoints for control plane + S2S IPsec for data plane) because it isolates control traffic, preserves predictable egress, and gives you a predictable failover path. Below I outline the tradeoffs and a checklist for netops.

Tradeoff summary (high level):
- VPC peering: lowest latency and simplest routing but requires cross-account route table management, exposes peered subnets (IP ownership concerns), and doesn't support cross-region. Not ideal if you need strong isolation or frequent environment churn.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strong isolation (service lives in our account), stable DNS-based access, fewer route table changes for you; we present the service via ENIs in our account so your IP blocks stay private. Slightly higher latency than peering (NIC hop) and you need to watch for SNAT behavior on egress.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): easiest from an ops standpoint to prototype, predictable source IPs if you allocate NAT on your edge, but higher and variable latency and more manual HA choreography. Good fallback / DR path.

Operational notes and gotchas:
- TCP session affinity and KV cache: long-lived connections benefit from peering/PrivateLink since the path stays local; overly aggressive NAT timeouts on your side can evict KV caches. Recommend explicit TCP idle-timeout >= 30 min for cache-sensitive endpoints.
- MTU/fragmentation: IPsec tunnels often reduce MTU (typically to ~1400); we recommend PMTU discovery tests during pilot traffic and to enable MSS clamping on your egress.
- Cross-account IAM & IP ownership: PrivateLink keeps the service in our account (we own ENIs) so your VPC IPs never need to be advertised; for peering you must add routes into your route tables referencing our prefixes — that requires governance.
- Monitoring & health: we push per-connection metrics and token-level latency traces to the Redwood Console; ensure your netops can accept syslog/flow logs for correlation (we provided a sample dashboard).

Attached: redwood-acacia-connectivity-playbook-v1.pdf (short checklist + diagrams).

Next steps I propose:
1) Technical alignment call with your netops (30m) — I'll invite Marcus (runtime lead) and Kim (security).
2) Execute a short pilot using PrivateLink + IPsec fallback; run a 48–72h load run to validate P95 and MTU.
3) If P95 < 75ms and KV coherence tests pass, we proceed with reserved capacity.

If you're OK with that flow I'll schedule the call for tomorrow.

— Vanessa Ortiz
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood-acacia-connectivity-playbook-v1.pdf
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai, marcus_lin@redwood.ai, connor_obrien@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-06-27T11:12:00-07:00
Subject: Internal: pilot matrix and runbook (internal only)

Internal notes — marking confidential: this is a terse technical matrix I sent to Vanessa for the call. Key items to confirm during the pilot:
- NAT design: if Acacia wants static source IPs we need to coordinate whether NAT happens on their edge or ours. If on our side (we provide egress NAT), list of allowed CIDRs must be provided and we'll add ACLs.
- BGP/peering: we should avoid cross-account BGP in phase 1; peering would require route propagation docs and acceptance tests.
- Failover: implement active route health checks on PrivateLink and scripted reconfig to flip to S2S if latency > 100ms for 3 consecutive mins.
- Observability hooks: add a synthetic probe (small 256b request) every 30s to measure tail latency and KV-hit rates; ingest into NET-1243 dashboard.

Attachments: acacia-topology-diff-annotated.png

— Kim
Engineering Manager, Private Deployments
Redwood Inference

From: Rajiv Narayan <rajiv@acaciahealth.com>
To: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
Cc: networking@acaciahealth.com, Samir Gupta <samir@acaciahealth.com>
Date: 2026-06-28T08:31:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pilot connectivity options — quick scoping questions

Appreciate the clear summary and the playbook. A couple follow-ups from netops:
- Encryption: will PrivateLink traffic be TLS-terminated on your side or do we need end-to-end TLS from our app -> Redwood runtime? We prefer end-to-end crypto for PHI-scope data.
- Cost predictability: PrivateLink shows up as interface endpoints in our account; are there additional per-GB or per-hour charges we should expect on your side for egress?
- Failover testing: can you share the scripted steps so our team can rehearse S2S failover?

If those answers look good we'll schedule the 48–72h run.

— Rajiv

From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>
To: Rajiv Narayan <rajiv@acaciahealth.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, marcus_lin@redwood.ai, connor_obrien@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-06-29T16:44:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Pilot connectivity options — quick scoping questions

Rajiv — short answers inline and then a final recommendation.

- Encryption: we recommend end-to-end TLS between your app and the Redwood runtime for PHI. PrivateLink encrypts the link at the ENI level but we will not terminate application TLS for PHI workloads; that stays end-to-end. For extra assurance we can enable mutual TLS (mTLS) between your service and our public TLS endpoint — we already support cert rotation via our KMS integration.

- Cost predictability: there are three cost centers to call out: (1) AWS interface endpoint hourly charges (in your account), (2) per-GB data processing on our side for egress (usage line on your estimate) and (3) any S2S egress if you choose to NAT through your edge. In the playbook we included an estimate table; we can convert it to a PO-friendly amount once we lock expected throughput.

- Failover steps: attached scriptable runbook (see Drive link: https://drive.redwood/reports/acacia-handoff-v1) — short version: health-probe -> traffic-shift -> monitor -> rollback. We'll coordinate a rehearsal window with your netops and run the script together.

Final recommendation (concise):
1) Phase 1 (pilot): PrivateLink (interface endpoint) for control and management plane traffic + active S2S IPsec tunnel(s) as a data-plane fallback. This gives you strong isolation for service control, stable DNS-based access, and a DR path without route-table churn.
2) NAT/Source IPs: prefer NAT on your edge for clearer audit trail. If you need static sources for allowlists, we can operate an egress NAT in our account but must add a small ACL and sign an operational SLA.
3) Validation: 48–72h run at expected TPS with synthetic probes; validate P95 < 75ms, MTU OK, and KV consistency.

I'll send a calendar invite for the technical alignment and the rehearsal window. If Acacia agrees to the pilot scope we'll prepare an SOW addendum for reserved capacity.

Thanks — looking forward to the run.

— Vanessa Ortiz
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
